content: 1. The effects of vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) on cognition remain inconclusive. Some studies have reported memory enhancement (Cramer 2001; Ghacibeh 2006), while others have found no change or even deterioration in memory (Helmstaedter 2001; Hoppe 2001; McGlone 2008). 2. A small randomized clinical trial demonstrated that administering VNS after learning improved word-recognition memory in individuals with epilepsy (Clark 1999). 3. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a medical device that delivers regular electrical stimulation to specific brain regions via implanted electrodes. 4. DBS is an FDA-approved treatment for Parkinson’s disease, dystonia, and essential tremor. 5. Research has shown that DBS is effective in reducing seizure frequency in epilepsy (Sprengers 2014). 6. Studies on DBS targeting the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT) have reported a 50% or greater reduction in mean seizure frequency in 16% to 100% of epilepsy patients (Hodaie 2002; Kerrigan 2004; Andrade 2006; Lim 2007; Osorio 2007). 7. A multicenter randomized trial of bilateral ANT stimulation in refractory partial epilepsy found that stimulated patients experienced a 40% reduction in seizure frequency compared to 14% in the control group (Fisher 2010). 8. Recent studies have explored the cognitive effects of DBS in epilepsy patients. One study on bilateral ANT stimulation found significant improvements in verbal fluency and delayed verbal memory tasks (Oh 2012). Another study showed that stimulation of the entorhinal region during learning significantly enhanced performance on a spatial learning task requiring navigation through a virtual environment (Suthana 2012). 9. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a non-invasive procedure that uses electromagnetic induction to deliver a magnetic field across the scalp, stimulating nerve cells in specific brain regions (Ališauskienė 2005). 10. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been extensively studied as a treatment for various psychiatric and neurological conditions, including depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, post-traumatic stress disorder, Parkinson’s disease, dystonia, and epilepsy (Rossi 2009). 11. Several small studies and case reports have demonstrated the efficacy of rTMS in reducing seizure frequency in refractory partial epilepsy (Tergau 1999; Menkes 2000; Joo 2007) and epilepsia partialis continua (Graff-Guerrero 2004; Misawa 2005; Rotenberg 2008). 12. Seven randomized controlled trials have evaluated the efficacy of TMS for seizure reduction in epilepsy. Four studies reported significant results (Tergau 2003; Fregni 2006; Wang 2008; Sun 2012), while three studies found no significant effects (Theodore 2002; Cantello 2007; Joo 2007). 13. One clinical trial (Fregni 2006) and one case report (Cotelli 2012) on rTMS in refractory epilepsy patients with cortical malformations found improvements in certain aspects of cognitive functioning. 14. The ketogenic diet is a high-fat, moderate-protein, low-carbohydrate diet used primarily in the treatment of refractory epilepsy, especially in children. 15. The ketogenic diet is based on a 3:1 or 4:1 fat-to-protein and carbohydrate ratio, mimicking the biochemical effects of fasting (Neal 2010). 16. A low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet induces a ketogenic state in the body, which has been associated with a reduction in seizure frequency (Huffman 2006). 17. Two systematic reviews of the ketogenic diet reported that approximately 16% of children achieve seizure freedom, and 33% to 56% experience a greater than 50% reduction in seizure frequency (Lefevre 2000; Keene 2006). 18. A randomized controlled trial found that the ketogenic diet significantly reduced seizure frequency in children, with 38% of those on the diet achieving a greater than 50% reduction in seizures compared to 6% in the control group (Neal 2010). 19. A recent Cochrane review (Levy 2012) identified four randomized controlled trials assessing the efficacy of the ketogenic diet. The review concluded that the diet offers shortto medium-term benefits, but long-term tolerability is low (Bergqvist 2005; Seo 2007; Kassoff 2008; Neal 2008). 20. Cognitive rehabilitation is a neuropsychological treatment program aimed at training attention and memory functions in individuals with cognitive deficits due to brain injury. 21. Although training strategies vary across programs, the primary goal of cognitive rehabilitation is compensation rather than restoration (Ponds 2006). 22. Compensatory strategies can be external or internal. External memory strategies involve storing information externally and using reminders, such as electronic agendas (Koorenhof 2012). Internal memory strategies focus on elaboration and visualization of information to facilitate later retrieval (Ponds 2006). 23. Research has demonstrated the effectiveness of cognitive rehabilitation programs in addressing epilepsy-related memory problems (Bresson 2007; Helmstaedter 2008; Radford 2011; Koorenhof 2012). 24. However, methodologies and program characteristics vary significantly across studies. 25. A randomized controlled trial comparing two cognitive rehabilitation programs—the retraining method and the compensation method—found both strategies to be effective in improving self-reported cognitive outcomes and quality of life in individuals with epilepsy (Engelberts 2002). 26. The mechanisms of action of vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) and its effects on memory are not fully understood. However, it is believed that VNS activates upstream neural networks from the vagus nerve input into the medulla and deep brain structures (George 2000). 27. Functional imaging studies suggest that the thalamus and mesial temporal lobe, which are involved in memory processes, are activated during VNS in patients with epilepsy and treatment-resistant depression (Lomarev 2002; Henry 2004). 28. Secondary benefits of VNS may include improved alertness and attentional capacities, as well as the potential for reduced antiepileptic drug (AED) use (Tatum 2001; Kostov 2009; Shahwan 2009). 29. The mechanisms of deep brain stimulation (DBS) are also not fully understood. Improvements in seizure control and potential cognitive benefits likely depend on the brain region targeted for neurostimulation and the interrelationships of neural networks with the stimulation targets. 30. DBS therapy in epilepsy has most frequently targeted the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT). 31. Three neuroanatomic circuits implicated in seizure propagation—the corticothalamic, mammillothalamic, and Papez circuits—are associated with the ANT (Mirski 1986; Takebayashi 2007; Lega 2010). 32. DBS may exert a positive, indirect effect on cognition by reducing abnormal epileptic activity within these pathways (Zhong 2011). 33. Recent research has shown that electrical stimulation during preoperative intracranial recording of the entorhinal cortex improved spatial memory in epilepsy patients (Suthana 2012). 34. In transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), an alternating electric current passes through a coil of wire, creating a rapidly changing magnetic field that is concentrated on a specific area depending on the coil shape (Hallett 2000). 35. When a TMS device is positioned, the magnetic field penetrates the skull and induces action potentials in nearby neurons, which may have excitatory or inhibitory effects (Hemond 2007).
